wine.name: Romanée-Conti
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Nuits, held whole by the domaine as a monopole
wine.sites: The single small vineyard of Romanée-Conti in the middle of the Vosne-Romanée slope, with La Romanée above it, Richebourg to the north, La Grande Rue to the south and Romanée-Saint-Vivant below.
wine.making: Picked by hand and sorted, fermented largely with whole bunches in open vats, then aged in new oak barrels, which the fruit absorbs, for well over a year before bottling at the domaine.
wine.glass: Rose petal, red cherry and wild strawberry over Chinese five spice, orange peel and forest floor; light in body yet deep, with silken, fine tannin and a long, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Supple enough to taste young but at its fullest after fifteen to twenty years, and a strong vintage lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant only to take an old bottle off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: Named for the Prince de Conti, who bought it in 1760, Romanée-Conti is the monopole of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, a single small grand cru in the middle of the Vosne-Romanée slope. Light in body yet long and perfumed, it wants a wide glass and time.
records.story: Monks of the priory of Saint-Vivant held vines on this slope in the Middle Ages, and by the seventeenth century the vineyard was known as La Romanée. In 1760 it was bought by Louis François de Bourbon, Prince de Conti (1717 to 1776), who outbid, the story goes, Madame de Pompadour (1721 to 1764), and who kept its wine, as it is told, for his own table; the vineyard came to carry his name. The Revolution took it from his heir and sold it at auction as national property. In 1869 it was bought by a Burgundian landowner whose heirs, the de Villaine family among them, built the domaine around it, and in 1933 the domaine added La Tâche, its second monopole. In 1942 the Leroy family bought into the domaine, which the two families have run together since as a société civile. Romanée-Conti kept its ungrafted vines through phylloxera until the harvest of 1945; they were pulled up, the vineyard was replanted in 1947, and it made no wine again until the early 1950s. For a sommelier it is the name every guest knows and few have tasted: a grand cru held whole by one domaine, light and endless rather than powerful.

wine.name: Chambertin
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Nuits
wine.sites: Parcels of Chambertin, the grand cru at the heart of the Gevrey slope below the woods, between Chambertin-Clos de Bèze to the north and Latricières-Chambertin to the south, on limestone under thin brown soil.
wine.making: Destemmed and fermented in open vats, then aged in new oak barrels, which the domaine keeps for its grands crus, for well over a year before bottling at the domaine.
wine.glass: Black cherry, liquorice and violet over iron, game and a savoury, earthy depth; firm, fine tannin and a long, deep finish, more power than charm when young.
wine.ageing: Tight and tannic for ten years or more, it opens slowly and lasts for decades in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one only off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The grand cru, its own appellation; the vineyard's name stands alone, with no village.

Bottled at the domaine, as the house has done since the 1930s.

records.table: Rousseau's Chambertin comes from the grand cru at the heart of the Gevrey slope, destemmed and raised in new oak. Dense, firm and savoury, and slower to open than the house's Clos de Bèze, it repays a decanter and a long wait.
records.story: Gevrey's great vineyard began with its neighbour: the monks of the abbey of Bèze planted Clos de Bèze in the seventh century, and Chambertin, the story goes, is the field of a peasant named Bertin who planted beside them, the champ de Bertin. By the eighteenth century its wine was famous far beyond Burgundy, and Napoleon, as the legend tells it, drank it at his campaigns, cut with water. In 1847 the village of Gevrey added the vineyard's name to its own. Armand Rousseau (1884 to 1959) inherited a few vines in the village at the start of the twentieth century and built the domaine by marriage and purchase, adding parcels of the grands crus. In the 1930s, urged on by a Paris wine writer, he began to bottle his own wine and sell it under his name, among the first growers of the Côte d'Or to do so, when most sold their wine in cask to the merchants of Beaune and Nuits. His son Charles (1923 to 2016) took over in 1959 and widened the holdings. Chambertin, firmer and slower than the house's Clos de Bèze, shows the domaine's method plainest: destemmed fruit, new oak kept for the grands crus, and patience.

wine.name: Musigny Grand Cru Vieilles Vignes
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Nuits
wine.sites: The domaine's larger part of Musigny, Les Petits Musigny entire among it, at the southern end of Chambolle beside the upper wall of the Clos de Vougeot, on thin limestone soil; the older vines alone go into this wine.
wine.making: Fermented in vats and aged in oak barrels, a share of them new, for well over a year before bottling at the domaine. Musigny vines too young for Vieilles Vignes go into the domaine's Chambolle-Musigny Premier Cru instead.
wine.glass: Red and black cherry, violet and rose over iron, liquorice and forest floor; silken and perfumed yet firmly built, with fine tannin and a long, slow finish.
wine.ageing: Reserved and tightly wound young, it shows its perfume only after a decade in bottle and lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: Only the older vines of de Vogüé's large share of Musigny, the grand cru at the southern end of Chambolle, go into its Musigny Vieilles Vignes. Reserved and tightly wound young, silken and perfumed with age, it rewards a decade's patience.
records.story: Since the fifteenth century the family has held vines in Chambolle, passing them down by descent and by marriage, and in 1766 a marriage brought the estate into the de Vogüé family. Comte Georges de Vogüé (1898 to 1987) ran it from 1925 for more than sixty years and gave it the name it bears. When the grands crus were drawn in the 1930s, Musigny was among them, and the domaine held the larger part of it, Les Petits Musigny entire. Musigny is also the one grand cru of the Côte de Nuits allowed to make white wine, and de Vogüé is its historic maker. After the white vines were replanted, the domaine sold that wine as Bourgogne Blanc from the 1994 vintage, and the Musigny name returned to its label with the 2015 vintage. Only the older red vines go into Musigny Vieilles Vignes; the younger make the domaine's Chambolle premier cru, so the grand cru carries the depth of old roots. Slow and structured, the face of Chambolle's perfume that opens only after ten years, it shows beside the house's Bonnes-Mares how one village can give two such different grands crus.

wine.name: Bonnes-Mares
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Nuits
wine.sites: Parcels on the Chambolle side of Bonnes-Mares, the grand cru that runs on into Morey-Saint-Denis at its northern end, drawn from both its soils: the terres rouges of reddish clay and the terres blanches of pale marl.
wine.making: Mostly destemmed, with whole bunches used sparingly, fermented in vats and aged in oak barrels with a restrained share of new wood for well over a year, then bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Black cherry, red currant and rose stem over crushed stone and a savoury earthiness; dense and firm for Chambolle, with fine, grippy tannin and a long, cool finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed young, it needs ten to fifteen years in bottle and lasts well beyond.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The grand cru, its own appellation, shared between Chambolle-Musigny and Morey-Saint-Denis.

records.table: Drawn from both the red clay and the pale marl of Bonnes-Mares, on the Chambolle side of the grand cru, Roumier's wine is firmer and darker than most Chambolle and restrained in its oak. It is slow to open, so keep it ten years and pour it with game.
records.story: Bonnes-Mares runs along the slope from Chambolle-Musigny into Morey-Saint-Denis, and its name is read either as the good mothers, the nuns of Tart who held land near by in the Middle Ages, or as an old word for well tilled ground. The domaine dates from 1924, when its founder came to Chambolle by marriage and his wife's family vines came with it. Like most growers of his day he sold much of his wine in cask to the merchants, and bottling at the domaine grew only slowly. Bonnes-Mares was ranked a grand cru when the appellations were drawn in the 1930s. The founder's son took charge in 1961, and the founder's grandson joined him in the early 1980s; by then the domaine held the walled Clos de la Bussière in Morey-Saint-Denis whole. Under the family the style has stayed restrained: whole bunches used sparingly, new oak held back, the fruit kept cool and fine. Bonnes-Mares is the domaine's largest grand cru holding, and it shows the house plainly, because the wine is drawn from both the red clay and the pale marl of the cru. Explain those two soils to a guest and you have explained why one vineyard can give two textures in a single wine.

wine.name: Clos de Tart
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Nuits, held whole by the domaine as a monopole
wine.sites: The walled clos itself, on the Morey-Saint-Denis slope between Clos des Lambrays and Bonnes-Mares, its rows planted across the slope rather than down it and picked in separate parcels.
wine.making: Picked by hand and vinified parcel by parcel, then aged in oak barrels for well over a year before the parcels are blended and the wine is bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and crushed violet over iron, liquorice and a savoury, stony depth; dark and firmly built, with dense, fine tannin and a long, cool finish.
wine.ageing: Dark and closed young, it opens after about ten years and lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: A walled grand cru held whole since Cistercian nuns acquired it in 1141, Clos de Tart is made entirely by the Domaine du Clos de Tart. Its rows run across the slope, and its wine is dark, firm and slow, so decant it an hour ahead.
records.story: In 1141 the nuns of Notre-Dame de Tart, a Cistercian house, acquired the vineyard on the slope of Morey and gave it their name. They held it for six and a half centuries, and in all that time it was never divided. The Revolution took it from them, and in 1791 it was sold at auction as national property to the Marey-Monge family, who kept it whole for more than a century. In 1932 it passed to the Mommessin family, merchants of the Mâconnais, and when the appellations of the Côte de Nuits were drawn it was ranked a grand cru in its own right. The Mommessin heirs sold it in 2017 to Artémis Domaines, so that in almost nine centuries the clos has known only a handful of owners. Its vines run across the slope, from north to south, the reverse of the usual Burgundian rows, and the domaine picks and vinifies them in parcels before it blends the wine; the younger vines go to a second wine, La Forge de Tart. Candidates learn it as the textbook monopole, with a founding year and a short line of owners; guests meet the dark, firm voice of Morey.

others.name: La Forge de Tart

traps: Clos de Tart is a full monopole; Clos des Lambrays, next door, is a near monopole.
Morey-Saint-Denis holds four grands crus wholly its own, Clos de Tart among them, plus the Morey slice of Bonnes-Mares.
Clos de Tart is not Clos de Vougeot: both are walled Cistercian vineyards, but Vougeot is split among many owners.

cards.front: Clos de Tart: who acquired the vineyard, and in what year?
cards.back: The Cistercian nuns of Notre-Dame de Tart, in 1141.

cards.front: How are the rows of Clos de Tart planted, and why is that unusual?
cards.back: Across the slope rather than up and down it, the reverse of the usual Burgundian layout.

questions.q: A guest notices that the rows of Clos de Tart run across the slope. What sets that layout apart?
opts: It is the reverse of the usual Burgundian rows
It is required of every Morey grand cru
It is required of every monopole in Burgundy
It copies the rows of Clos de Vougeot
questions.exp: Most Burgundy vines run up and down the slope; Clos de Tart's rows run across it, the reverse of the usual layout, and no rule requires it of a monopole or a grand cru.

questions.q: Clos de Tart has changed hands very rarely since 1141. Which family held it from 1932 until 2017?
opts: The Mommessin family
The Marey-Monge family
The de Vogüé family
The Leroy family
questions.exp: The Mommessin family bought it in 1932 and sold it to Artémis Domaines in 2017; the Marey-Monge family held it from the Revolution until 1932.

sources.title: The Sommelier's Codex: the library records of Clos de Tart

report: No page or search was open to the author or to the refuter: the search budget shared by the run was spent and the network refuses every host, so the record's one https source is the Codex's own library, read in place, as in chunks f2 and f3; the refuter's reading is in reviews/check-f1.json.

From the library or the Codex: 1141 and the nuns of Tart, the monopole held whole, the Mommessin family from 1932, the sale to Artémis Domaines in 2017, the rows across the slope, the parcels, La Forge de Tart from the younger vines, Lambrays as a near monopole, Morey's four grands crus.

From the author's reading, unconfirmed here: the sale at the Revolution in 1791 to the Marey-Monge family, the walls built by the nuns, the vineyard's neighbours (Lambrays and Bonnes-Mares), the Mommessins as Mâconnais merchants.
The year Clos de Tart was ranked grand cru (1939 in the author's recollection) is left as when the appellations were drawn.
The library calls the nuns Bernardine; the record calls them Cistercian, which the Codex's own question also does (the Bernardines were a Cistercian order), and both are true.

changed: story: They walled it is cut: who built the wall was not confirmed, while the nuns' holding of six and a half centuries, 1141 to 1791, stands.
